title: Do Verifiers Reduce Security‑Relevant Misconfigurations? A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Verifier‑in‑the‑Loop GVR for Intent→Configuration
abstract: We preregistered and executed a deterministic paired experiment to test whether embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop reduces security‑increasing (forbidden‑reachability) misconfigurations produced by an LLM‑driven intent→configuration pipeline. Under a frozen paired design (N=300 matched intents; 150 benign seeds + 150 programmatic adversarial variants) and a shared_initial_candidate generation contract (one LLM candidate replayed to both arms to conserve provider calls), the run completed all planned episodes (600 episodes; model_calls_used = 300). Confirmatory outcome: baseline_success = 300 and guarded_success = 300 (contingency n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0); McNemar exact two‑sided p = 1.0; bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) 95% CI for paired risk‑difference = [0.0, 0.0]. No validator reported forbidden reachability and the repair step was never invoked. A one‑sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound on an undetected baseline violation rate is ≈ 0.00994. Because the repair path was unexercised, these results show that inserting a verifier does not change observed compliance when baseline generation already satisfies the safety predicate under the chosen contract; they do not demonstrate that verifier‑guided repair can rescue genuine violations. We archive preregistration, execution accounting, per‑episode validator traces, and analysis artifacts to support reproducibility and to guide follow‑up stress tests targeted at exercising repair.

sections.introduction:
LLMs can automate intent‑driven network configuration but risk producing changes that increase attack surface or violate access‑control policies. Prior system and survey work therefore recommends constrained generation, execution oracles, and iterative generate–verify–repair (GVR) loops as mitigations. Yet, preregistered confirmatory evidence that a verifier placed inside a GVR loop meaningfully reduces security‑increasing misconfigurations under adversarial inputs is limited.

Research question. Does embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a GVR loop reduce the incidence of forbidden‑reachability misconfigurations produced by an LLM intent→configuration pipeline?

Contributions. We (1) preregistered a paired confirmatory design (cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1) and executed it deterministically in a Dockerized FRRouting‑style emulation, (2) report complete, artifact‑grounded outcomes for N=300 matched intents under a shared_initial_candidate contract (model_calls_used = 300), (3) provide compact, reproducible numeric results showing a degenerate contingency (n11=300) together with a descriptive Clopper–Pearson upper bound on undetected baseline violations (≈0.00994), and (4) derive artifact‑supported design lessons and recommendations for experiments that intend to exercise repair.
sections.related_work: Three threads motivate our design. First, generate–verify–repair and execution‑guided repair architectures improve correctness in code and IaC tasks by using verifier feedback to guide repairs; system work (e.g., TerraFormer) shows verifier strength and repair strategies are decisive for realized gains. Second, comprehensive surveys and NetOps papers document LLM failure modes (hallucination, overconfidence, domain mismatch) and recommend validators, constrained generation, or human oversight for operational risk reduction. Third, emulation and testbed research demonstrates that execution‑based validation is feasible for research evaluation but warns of external‑validity gaps relative to production networks. Our study aims at a tightly scoped, preregistered paired test that (a) fixes generation semantics, (b) accounts deterministically for provider calls, and (c) archives per‑episode validator traces for auditability.
sections.methodology:
Design and preregistration. The preregistered confirmatory design (study cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1) specified a paired binary design with N=300 matched intents (150 benign seeds and 150 programmatic adversarial variants). The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; the planned confirmatory test is an exact McNemar two‑sided test (alpha=0.05). Sensitivity analyses and missingness treatments were prespecified in the preregistration.

Generation semantics and adapter contract. To limit provider cost under the adapter contract (maximum_model_calls = 600 allowed), we preregistered and executed a shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each paired intent we generated a single LLM candidate and replayed that identical candidate to both arms (baseline is therefore a replayed candidate rather than an independent draw). This choice produced model_calls_used = 300 for 300 pairs; the provider‑call audit records the stage_counts key 'shared_initial_generation' = 300.

Intervention arms and repair policy. Baseline = shared initial candidate replayed directly. Guarded = same initial candidate validated by deterministic validators; if any validator reports the forbidden‑reachability predicate, the GVR policy allows up to one repair LLM call (max one repair per pair). Repair prompts were invoked only on validator‑detected violations; across this run no repair call was issued because validators never flagged violations.

Precise predicate and validators (concise technical definition). Forbidden‑reachability predicate: for each task the task manifest encodes per‑task constraints (task_payload.constraints) including protected_interfaces and workflow policies; we treat a configuration as violating when it enables any reachability relation disallowed by that task‑level constraint set (i.e., any task‑declared forbidden pair becomes reachable under the applied configuration). This formulation keeps the predicate task‑scoped and machine‑verifiable; per‑task forbidden pairs and protected_interfaces (for example, the canonical protected interface 'mgmt1') are encoded in execution/task_manifest.jsonl.

Validators and decision rule (summary). Two deterministic validators were used: (1) a containerized execution validator that applies the candidate configuration in a Dockerized FRRouting‑style emulation and computes observed reachability (execution‑guided simulation), and (2) a lightweight static graph‑based reachability analyzer that reasons over normalized CLI commands to detect topology/policy consequences. We combined validator outputs with a logical‑OR decision rule: a pair is labeled 'violating' if any validator reports forbidden reachability. Per‑episode validator_traces record each validator's judgment and version (validator_id = 'deterministic_netops_validator_v5', validator_version = '5.0'). Full per‑episode traces and validator outputs are archived for inspection.

Reproducibility and artifact pointers (short). The complete artifact bundle (preregistration, execution manifest, raw model responses, per‑episode validator traces, provider‑call audit, and analysis outputs) is archived in the evidence bundle. Representative verification files include execution/execution_manifest.json (execution accounting), execution/raw_results.jsonl (raw per‑episode results), execution/task_manifest.jsonl (task inputs and per‑task constraints), analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (primary contingency), and analysis/condition_summary.csv (condition summaries). The initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256 included in the Disclosure Statement). Detailed manifests and hashes are preserved in the evidence bundle; we keep the paper narrative compact and point to these canonical artifacts for full verification.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. Planned episodes = 600 (300 pairs × 2 conditions); completed episodes = 600; failed episodes = 0. Provider‑call accounting under the shared_initial_candidate semantics: model_calls_used = 300 (execution manifest records 'shared_initial_generation' = 300). The run interval is recorded in the execution manifest.

Primary confirmatory outcome (compact). The paired contingency is n11 = 300, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (Table 1). Baseline_success_count = 300; guarded_success_count = 300. Paired risk‑difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the paired risk‑difference (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Because no violations were observed in N=300 initial candidates, a one‑sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound on the (true) baseline violation probability is ≈ 0.00994.

Repair activity and verifier concordance. No validator reported forbidden reachability for any initial candidate, so no repair prompt was invoked (repair_applied flags = false in every per‑episode validator_trace). Verifier disagreement rate across the two validators is 0 in the archived artifacts.

Representative examples. Representative shared initial candidates and matching validator_traces for medium/hard tasks are archived (e.g., execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt and execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json) and illustrate the shared playback semantics and deterministic validator outputs.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation. Under the exact adapter contract (shared_initial_candidate), declared model (gpt‑5‑mini), two deterministic validators combined by logical OR, emulator, and the programmatic adversarial perturbation generator used here, baseline generation satisfied the forbidden‑reachability predicate for all sampled intents; therefore inserting the verifier did not change observed compliance. The archived artifacts (execution accounting, per‑episode validator traces, and the paired contingency) jointly support this narrow statement.

Why the confirmatory test is uninformative about repair efficacy. The paired McNemar test relies on discordant pairs to detect difference; with n10 = n01 = 0 there are no discordant pairs and McNemar inference about repair efficacy is uninformative. Two coupled design facts caused this degeneracy: (a) the shared_initial_candidate contract reduces independent‑sample variance between arms (one LLM draw per pair) and (b) under the chosen model/validators the adversarial perturbations did not produce validator‑detectable forbidden reachability. Consequently the experiment answers whether verifier insertion changes compliance when baseline is already compliant under the chosen contract—not whether verifier‑guided repair can rescue violations.

Design lessons (artifact‑grounded). (1) Generation semantics matter: independent‑condition generation (two LLM draws per pair) increases the chance of observing discordant violating outputs that repair could correct but doubles model_calls (from 300→600 under the same adapter budget). (2) Adversary potency matters: stronger or targeted adversaries against verifier predicates are required to exercise repair. (3) Verifier diversity and strength matter: richer oracles and production‑grade execution checks are needed to stress different failure modes. (4) Reproducibility is practical: archived per‑episode traces, provider audit, and bootstrap parameters (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) enable deterministic reanalysis and targeted follow‑ups.

Threats to validity (concise). Internal validity: shared_initial_candidate reduces independent sampling; single‑model scope limits generality. Construct validity: whether task‑declared forbidden pairs and the two validators fully capture operational security risk is uncertain (per‑task constraints are in execution/task_manifest.jsonl). External validity: synthetic tasks and Dockerized FRRouting emulation may not reflect production heterogeneity. Conclusion validity: degenerate contingency violates preregistered power assumptions. Each threat is linked to archived artifacts to enable targeted remediation.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired evaluation of a verifier‑in‑the‑loop GVR pipeline for intent→configuration generation (declared LLM gpt‑5‑mini; two deterministic validators; shared_initial_candidate semantics). The run completed N=300 matched pairs with model_calls_used = 300 and produced a degenerate outcome: baseline and guarded arms both passed the forbidden‑reachability predicate on all pairs (n11 = 300). Because no validator‑reported violations occurred, the repair path was never invoked and the experiment cannot evaluate whether verifier‑guided repair rescues violating outputs. The principal scientific takeaway is methodological: generation semantics, adversary design, repair budget, verifier strength, and model diversity materially determine whether a verifier‑in‑the‑loop architecture can be shown to reduce security‑relevant misconfigurations. We release the preregistration and deterministic execution artifacts to enable reproducible follow‑up stress tests specifically designed to exercise the repair path (independent draws, stronger adversaries, multi‑model comparisons, and richer oracles).

limitations: Degenerate confirmatory outcome: zero discordant pairs (n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0) render McNemar inference uninformative about repair efficacy because no repair opportunities were observed despite the preregistered power calculation assuming a nonzero baseline violation rate.

GVR not exercised: validators never reported forbidden reachability under the chosen model/validators/adversary, so the repair path was never invoked; the experiment tests whether verifier insertion changes compliance when baseline is already compliant, not whether verifier‑guided repair rescues violations.

Generation contract choice: shared_initial_candidate semantics reduced model‑call overhead (model_calls_used = 300) but limited independent draws that could produce discordant errors; independent‑condition generation or increased repair budgets would better exercise repair.
Adversarial potency: the programmatic adversarial variants used here did not trigger validator‑detectable forbidden reachability; stronger or targeted adversaries are needed to exercise repair paths.
External validity: tasks were synthetic and executed in Dockerized FRRouting‑style emulation; results may not generalize to heterogeneous production devices, live traffic, or operator workflows.

Model and verifier scope: a single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) and two deterministic validators were evaluated; other LLMs, stronger or different verifiers, or ensemble oracles may produce different outcomes.
